description: We are Space10, from Türkiye. We will use NASA sources to create illustrated stories about equipment left on the Moon and Mars. We combine scientific accuracy with imagination, drawing, and narration. Our team values curiosity, research, creative writing, and collaboration.
summary:
One Small Slip: The Spatula Lost in Space is an animated, click-through picture book about a real object lost in space: the spatula astronaut Piers Sellers lost during a spacewalk on NASA's STS-121 mission in July 2006. The spatula tells its own story, from a kitchen drawer to astronaut training, launch, the moment it slips away, life among orbital debris, and its fiery return through the atmosphere. Speech bubbles pop up one by one, scenes move, and pages turn with a click, so the book works both as a live presentation and as a self-paced story. It is available in English and Turkish.

We used humor to make a serious topic memorable. Behind the jokes are real facts: objects in orbit travel at about 28,000 km/h, even a tiny paint fleck can chip a spacecraft window, and that is why astronauts tether their tools. A final "What really happened?" page separates fiction from verified facts.

Space debris is a growing risk for satellites and crewed missions. By turning one lost spatula into a story, our project helps children and the public understand why every object left in orbit matters, and why we need to keep space clean.
details:
What it does

One Small Slip is an animated, click-through picture book about space debris, told by a real lost object: the spatula astronaut Piers Sellers lost during the third spacewalk of NASA's STS-121 mission on July 12, 2006. Over 11 pages, the spatula narrates its journey from a kitchen drawer to astronaut training, launch, the moment it slips away, life among orbital debris, and its fiery return through the atmosphere. A final page, "What really happened?", lists the verified facts. A 7-slide demo summarizes the project.

How it works

Each click (or the space bar, or a swipe on phones) shows the next speech bubble. When a page's dialogue is finished, the page turns with a paper-flip animation. Bubbles can play automatically or wait for the presenter. The characters include astronauts, Mission Control, a bolt, a paint fleck, a retired satellite and even Earth.

Benefits and impact

Space debris is hard to care about because nobody sees it. A funny, personal story makes the topic easy to remember for children and the general public. Real science is woven into the jokes: orbital speed (about 28,000 km/h), why a tiny paint fleck can chip a window, why astronauts tether their tools, 16 sunrises a day, how thin the atmosphere is, and how small objects burn up on reentry. Teachers can present it in class in a few minutes. It is free, works on any device and is available in English and Turkish.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file. All illustrations are SVG drawn in code and animated with CSS. No installation or libraries are needed; fonts come from Google Fonts, and the project is hosted on GitHub Pages. We used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help write and translate the story, generate the illustration and animation code, and check facts against news sources.

Creativity

Instead of a list of facts, the lost object tells its own story. Kitchen humor becomes a set of metaphors: Earth as a blue pancake, the atmosphere as a thin layer of oil in a pan, and reentry as the biggest frying pan in the world.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: fiction and facts are clearly separated, and because the astronauts' dialogue is invented, they are not named inside the story. Respect: the book is dedicated to Piers Sellers, who died in 2016. We also considered age-appropriate humor, accessibility (keyboard controls, screen-reader text, reduced-motion support, a phone layout) and keeping the presentation short.
